column2: - U2: a project-scope policy symlink target is not on the floor. The work-project AGENTS.md copy waits for an idle session to refresh.
- E1: nothing in the catch ledger may change review practice, models, roles or spend until a seeded-defect control and a clean-patch control run.
- L5: a broken hook symlink exits 127 before its fail-open code runs; the adoption hook is not role-gated to the seat.
- S1/S2: display and encoding follow-ups (lossless `Cwd:` encoding, desk path display, escape-token helper, look-alike dashes, display package, 16× pre-cap, CLI rendering test).
- Requirements: the rail proves marker identity, not clause coverage (open question 6b); work-project's rail copy has 193 rows off form; basketball-geek has 2.
- Edge desk: nothing bounds the total size of the blocks one tool returns; a narrowed desk spawn drops the MCP servers and pi's other built-ins.
- pi 1.0: the seed's `asyncByDefault: true` restates upstream (drop it at the next seed revision, R-361 diff first).
- Review-ledger lane: strengthen the non-mutating-`check` test with a stale sentinel.
- Tranche 3: the land helper does not defend a branch switch in the main checkout mid-merge; reviews refuse repositories with submodules.
- Tranche 4: the acceptance gate prints nothing on a pass.
- Tranche 5: uninstall's preview stops at a loaded desk; its ancestor checks are preflight-only.
- Tranche 6: per-check SKIPs inside a test file stay invisible to the rail; nothing keeps future pi tests on the locator; the owner's Windows machine passed the install-and-hooks check on 2026-10-16.
- Knowledge ruling: a review-test fixture can loop forever.
- Tranche 2: the trial rubric scores only decisions the extractor finds. Full list: the 2026-10-07 session entry.
- `~/nana-agent-loop` still tracks the retired hook's empty `.claude/.context-warned`.

- Four-digit IDs: work-project's hand copy of the rail still reads three digits (hand edit, no urgency); basketball-geek is on the older pytest-marker rail, so taking the new tag is a migration. The rails sort ID lists as text (cosmetic). A character outside the shared whitespace list between a row's opening pipe and its ID hides the row from both rails.

- Land rule: the helper checks that every recorded verdict is LAND, not who reviewed; the round records are a plain file; a narrow review counts for everything up to its revision; a direct commit to main bypasses it (the working pattern forbids that). Every revision reviewed before the land rule needs a fresh review.
- Install check: it proves install and hooks in a temporary home, not a live Claude Code session. Linux runs no install check.

- Review standard: projects other than nana-pi take the new working-pattern text only when `nana-setup project` runs there. `review-ledger run` gets no standard. Nothing stages a pi-review change before it reaches every caller.

- Fresh install: the desk's two install hints in its code and the study README still name no cutoff, since the owner froze the desk. We tested PowerShell 7, and the Windows install check runs the README's pi install in cmd (readme-windows-checklist). PowerShell 5.1 should pass the unquoted cutoff unchanged, but nobody has run it.

- Process lane reviews left two requirements whose tests check less than their rows say: an unreadable standard file, and each preamble rule on its own line. A third, step 8's trust target, is now checked by the readme-install lane's last-step test.

- CI pin: the install gate checks the workflow text, not the resolved packages; a check that imports pi after install is the hardening step. The cutoff does not freeze deprecations or retags. The suite's template acceptance test needs the network, and a network hiccup refused one land run.

- Claude Code hooks on Windows: uninstall still refuses there, and its leftover-entry report would miss the new form (the Windows install-shape lane). On Windows, doctor prints the six hook settings rows and no hook-file row (win-hook-rows). On the Windows CI leg, three file-mode checks and one test that deletes its own working folder stay red (test portability). Nothing here proves how Claude Code itself starts the hooks, routes PowerShell, or how long they take.

- Windows pi launch: nana runs the first `pi.com`, `.exe`, `.bat` or `.cmd` on PATH — not PowerShell's `pi.ps1`, an alias or a function, and never a `pi.cmd` in the working folder. A `.cmd` pi whose path or package folder holds `%`, `!` or a double quote needs a manual `pi install`. Since win-pi-launch-orphan, this holds only for a pi with no npm package beside it. Post-edit calls a missing tool a failed check when it hides behind a non-simple first word or later in a compound command. A failing command led by an internal command outside the sealed list reads as "could not run".

- Verdict reader: a plain first-line LAND followed by a rejection that avoids the word "verdict" still reads LAND. Look-alike letters outside the fold table and misspelled labels are not caught. The reader ignores a middle verdict line when the final line carries one. Notes that say "verdict" after a first-line verdict leave the round empty. yokai-world's nine empty records from before the fix stay; a session merged those revisions by hand.

- Roster: for a lane, the Windows evidence is a fake pi package in CI. No real pi has run a lane through the new launch on Windows. Since install-check-review-launch, CI's Windows install check runs a real pi review through both installed pi-review launchers. That review runs offline with a test model; no real model has reviewed there. The launchers refuse pi.dev's managed install, pnpm and Volta 2 with a named reason. On Windows, review-ledger run now starts an npm-installed pi too. Since review-ledger-run-win-launch, it starts an npm-installed claude there as well. The launchers retry a refusal like any failed attempt. A test pins that pi-worker writes the refusal to its output file; none pins pi-review's write. The tests-first reds never ran alone on Windows, because the pull request had merge conflicts. No row pins that a non-lane pi-worker reads no roster. The frozen desk refuses to save a user file holding a roster.

- Seat guide: a rule line cannot prove a seat obeys it; only the owner's Windows seat will show that. An unattended Claude Code session stops background commands after 30 minutes by default, so a seat there would lose a long build. A pi seat waits on its one foreground command. Two plan review notes stay as they are. The runtime table names only the two older Claude rules. The guide's line on the seat's own fixes covers one-line fixes only.

- Tree: existing projects keep their flat ledger until the lift. The report's packets fail for a project in a subfolder of a repo, and its title and default output name still say nana-pi. Projects get no tree gate in their own suites, and nothing flags a seed's DRAFT purposes. The checker skips rows inside code fences, where the rail counts them.

- Lift: nana-pi's general-engineering rows still sit in its own feature, so the lift's default refuses nana-pi until a later lane decides where they go. Since 2026-10-16 the lift carries shares and changes one only where the mapping declares it. A blank `Also applies:` line survives a lift, though the shares row says no line should stay. A regroup that splits a section with prose between table fragments puts that prose above one table. yokai-world needs a hand fix or a hand-written grouping, and trading-zone keeps its engineering capability mid-file until its regroup. An edit another session makes between the final re-read and the rename is lost; git still holds the pre-lift ledger. On Windows a rename can fail while antivirus holds the new file, and nobody has run the PowerShell form there. The lift refuses some honest shapes rather than lifting them: a flat ledger whose intro has a field-labelled line, a requirement table with a blank line before its first row, and a fenced example holding a sample row. Nineteen secondary checks have no test of their own; an independent check judged each one covered by a pinned check.

- Regroup: the page's two long rows list more parts than every test checks; after four builds the seat closed the build list and recorded the rest in `docs/reviews/regroup-2026-10-15/seat-verify-8c7ed24.md`. A merge into a shared row's home, or a row moved into the feature that shares it, needs a share verdict. sol's round-3 plan point was declined: a move the reviewer refused and the drafter turned into a share keeps that history in the share's reason. Its evidence-through-a-link test passes without testing on a Windows machine that cannot create links.

- Roster notice: nobody has looked at the notice in either app yet. pi's panel stays until the next reset and wraps at 80 columns. A relative agent folder shows "roster unknown". Two providers that serve one model name look the same in it. The Windows-only hook checks run only in CI's Windows leg. On a case-sensitive macOS volume, a path spelled in another letter case still shows as `~`.

- Roster set: the one-command slot change takes no lock, so a desk save, install or editor write during it is lost. It keeps one backup only, and the next write replaces it. On a machine with no roster, its first change writes the whole default roster. Later default changes then stop reaching that machine until the owner copies the backup back. Its refusal inside a pi model's shell is advisory; a model that clears the variable, and pi older than 0.82.0, pass it. Nobody has checked the pi version on the owner's Windows machine. The change must be the command's first word; after the JSON flag it changes nothing. It checks only the roster, not the gate settings. A hard-linked file loses its other link, and no test pins the kept file mode. On Windows, a program holding the file open can fail the rename; run it again.

- Roster set (review): every change writes an empty larger-builder slot. A second machine whose checkout predates that slot then refuses the roster until it pulls. The README no longer warns of this. Copying the backup back recovers it.
- Roster set (review): the default-roster check types the defaults out by hand instead of reading them by name. Retuning a default then fails that check as well as the one that pins it.
- Roster set (review): no check runs the temp file through a symlinked roster. The README names three refusals, but read and write failures also refuse.

- Project files: the AGENTS.md refresh retries a refused rename three times, 20 ms apart, a chosen bound; a longer Windows lock still ends in "could not safely replace AGENTS.md". The refresh re-checks AGENTS.md just before each retry; a save in the instant between that check and the rename can still be lost, since Windows has no atomic compare-and-replace. On Windows the owner-swap check skips when the test cannot swap the file itself. Existing projects on macOS keep their CLAUDE.md link, which `--check` still accepts.
- Gate tests on Windows: the desk leg of the agent-folder parity test and the live-working-folder case skip there.
- Lane write guard (win-gate-tmp): on macOS the guard refuses the lane typed through its data-volume firmlink path, as main did.

- Lane write guard (win-gate-tmp): run on its own, the guard's test builds its fixtures in the real home and removes them on exit. One build run left a folder there. Nobody knows why, and the folder is gone now.

- Lane write guard (win-gate-tmp): no test covers long-path prefixes, Git Bash drive paths, driveless paths or the plain real-path fallback. On Linux every spelling check skips in the suite, because the suite's home sits under a temp folder. The gate keeps its own path resolver beside the review tools' one.

- Lane write guard temp folders (lane-guard-temp-root, independent check): a home inside the OS temp folder now turns off temp output there on macOS and Windows. The guard sets that temp folder aside because it holds home. The change fails closed, and /tmp still works on macOS and Linux. Run alone with its home inside the temp folder, the guard's test file turns two older checks red. The suite stays green, because its runner puts home and the temp folder side by side.

- Lane write guard temp folders (lane-guard-temp-root, independent check): the new shared temp-folder module's containment helper takes the outer folder first. The gate's own private helper takes it second. The gate also keeps its own copy of the module's path resolver. Nothing breaks today, but a later caller could pass the folders in the wrong order. The rm-outside-asks module uses the shared helper, and its checks fail if the order flips.
- Lane write guard temp folders (lane-guard-temp-root, plan): a broad temp folder, like a mount point or the lane worktrees' parent, still counts. Only a root or a folder holding home is set aside.
- Lane write guard temp folders (lane-guard-temp-root, plan): on macOS and Linux the guard counts only the temp folder Node picks. It ignores the other two temp settings.
- Lane write guard temp folders (lane-guard-temp-root, plan): a refusal names the lane boundary but not the temp folder the guard set aside.

- Lane write guard temp folders (lane-guard-temp-root, wrong-code pairs): on macOS and Linux no check sets home through a link. So a guard that compares home as typed survives there. The Windows leg catches it through the runner's short name. No check sets a temp folder whose path is a text prefix of home's path but does not hold home. So a text-prefix containment test survives everywhere; it would wrongly refuse, never wrongly allow. No check makes a folder's lookup on disk fail. So the guard's fallback to comparing names goes untested; a guard without it survives.

- Lane write guard temp folders (lane-guard-temp-root, final review): on macOS and Linux /tmp is its own rule and always counts. With home inside /tmp, as on some Linux runners, home stays writable to a lane. Main behaves the same. The pack README now says /tmp counts regardless.

- Lane write guard temp folders (lane-guard-temp-root, final review): on Windows a temp setting of a bare drive letter and colon names that drive's current folder, not its root. So the guard does not set it aside. Nobody sets such a value in practice.
- Lane write guard temp folders (lane-guard-temp-root, both reviews): the guard's test file makes a folder and a link and never removes them. Each run leaves both in the temp folder.

- Lane write guard temp folders (lane-guard-temp-root, final review): on macOS the guard compares folder identity only along home's ordinary path. So the system data volume and the two folders above it still count as temp folders. A temp setting naming the data volume lets a lane write reach home through that spelling. No honest tool sets that.

- Lane write guard temp folders (lane-guard-temp-root, final review): a volume that reports inode zero for every folder would make the guard refuse temp output. That fails closed. Some FAT or network volumes may do this (inferred).

- Session start on Windows: the objective test runs 982 checks there against 1,236 on Linux; the difference is whole groups of POSIX-only cases (unreadable files, named pipes, file ownership, directory modes), each declared by one printed SKIP line. A hostile path shown in the objective block doubles each backslash on Windows, the block's quoting rule. CI's macOS leg once failed the shared mutation runner's killed-shard cleanup check on another lane's run; it passes locally and is a candidate flaky check.

- Claude hooks on Windows: the deleted-working-folder case and the POSIX mode-bit and legacy-migration checks skip there, by design; the render test pins a Windows-legal hostile name in place of the names NTFS refuses.

- Line endings: a CRLF file a Windows editor saves inside nana-pi becomes LF at commit, by design. The Python template's trace check on CRLF files skips when uv cannot fetch pytest. An existing Windows clone keeps its CRLF files until its owner re-checks it out once (see Open for the owner).

- Runtime map: on Windows nothing tests a stop, the stop does not end the suite's tree, and short, linked and native forms of the repository path are not mapped; Linux's process listing is untested. Two measurements at once are not guarded. A coverage folder set by hand to an empty or relative path, an unreadable coverage file and hand-damaged data get no special handling. Copies run from a temporary folder and children stopped by a signal are not counted, and the impact view says so in its closing line.

- Mutation runner: the seat skipped the lane's own 43-pair run under the owner's 2026-10-17 ruling; the table is committed and applies cleanly. Its one timing check (the stagger) may fail on a loaded machine. The shared runner has judged no pair on Windows, and nobody has seen the dead-run cleanup work there. A parent killed outright cleans nothing and leaves its lock for the next run to replace. A table's config values are not type-checked, and a hung git call hangs its part of the run. The runner and the suite still each hold their own copy of the child setup and the tree kill; the parallel suite lane kept both. Older lanes keep their copied runners.

- Mutation runner: its cleanup check failed once in 44 runs on CI's Windows leg. That check runs at one and three parts, then with one part killed, and expects nothing left running. Since mutation-runner-win-prune, the runner removes a refused scratch worktree itself and retries. Its parts also take turns to add and remove worktrees. The Windows leg passed once on that lane's tip. Whether the failure is gone needs more Windows runs. The Windows leg now blocks release, so a repeat failure blocks a release.

- Feature-first rules: other projects get the new shared section only when `nana-setup project` runs there again; their Claude rules change at once through the links on macOS and Linux, and on Windows at the next install. pi's reviewer seed still asks for edge cases in its plan section, and a machine keeps its old seed. The small-lane builder stopped the lane's first build after five minutes with no commit and no reason; a Claude Sonnet 5 builder finished it.

- Seat rule: a rule line cannot prove a seat obeys it. Seats on macOS and Linux read the new guide at once through its link; a Windows seat gets it only when `nana-setup install` runs there again. The planning slot does not say a planned lane has no worktree. The plan's pair check copies the pointer check rather than running it.

- Handoff tests on Windows: NTFS refuses LF, ESC, tab and `:` in a name, so those hostile names are POSIX-only cases. Windows runs a Unicode line separator and a bidi override in their place. Windows cannot hold a home of about 290 characters, so no test checks the long-home pointer cap there. The product never shortens a path that holds `~`. So on a machine whose home folder has a short 8.3 name, the pointer shows the full path. A test must not use `fs.mkdirSync`'s return value as a path: on Windows it comes back as `\\?\C:\...`, which cmd.exe refuses as a working folder. The store test's symlink probe tries only a junction, so on Windows without Developer Mode its file symlink fails instead of skipping.

- Install on Windows: the retired quoted context hook is never removed on Windows, because no Windows install ever wrote it. The seat's skip audit left smaller items in `docs/reviews/win-install-shape-2026-10-17/seat-skip-audit.md`: some comments and requirement tags in these tests still describe the macOS shape.

- Hook rows on Windows (win-hook-rows): a few code comments still say install skips the hook files on Windows. Install now prints no hook-file row there. Their point, that Windows gets no hook file, still holds. No user sees them.

- Hook rows on Windows (win-hook-rows): the two new checks look for the hook scripts' file names. A Windows row relabelled without its file name passes both. Only the Windows install check's list of allowed doctor notes would catch such a doctor row.
- Hook rows on Windows (win-hook-rows): no check runs the install dry run on Windows. It uses the same hook step. The independent check saw it print no hook-file row.

- Hook rows on Windows (win-hook-rows, install-cli-pins): the check that every macOS and Linux only step creates nothing on Windows names the two such steps today, the hook folder and the desk service. A step added later needs its own case.

- Occupied skill folder on Windows: one older install requirement is still worded for every skill folder. On Windows it now holds only for nana-setup's own copy of the requirements skill. The install-pins lane replaced the other three.

- Occupied skill folder on Windows: install refuses an unmarked folder that matches no shipped version. That covers a hand-edited older copy, a copy saved with a byte-order mark and an empty folder. Install names the folder and asks the owner to move it; nothing is lost. Nobody has checked the copy on the owner's Windows machine.

- Occupied skill folder on Windows: the ownership check's comment says it never follows a link. Its compare with the pack does read through a linked file. It only reads, so it writes nothing through the link.
- Occupied skill folder on Windows: no test pins that a run adding only the ownership marker reports a change. The seat's wrong-code pair for it survived.

- Occupied skill folder on Windows (review): no check ties the list of shipped skill versions to git history. If another lane changes the requirements skill and lands first, install on Windows refuses a copy made from that commit until someone adds its key. Nothing is lost; install exits 1 and names the folder.

- Setup tools on Windows: the launchd desk checks skip there, since the desk service is macOS-only. GNU tar unquotes the folder after `-C` when it extracts, so a backslash path such as `C:\Users\...\new` breaks there. The README's restore line is safe in Git Bash, where `~` becomes a forward-slash path. The restore test's leak check compares raw bytes, so on Windows it cannot see a source path stored with escaped backslashes. When a test forces doctor's platform to macOS on Windows, doctor still calls `process.getuid`, which Windows lacks.

- Review tools and folder spellings: an item reviewed on a Windows seat before this change restarts its round count once, since its key now uses the folder's spelling on disk. A firmlink-typed review output on macOS behaves as before. Nothing tests the key's fallback for a git too old for absolute paths, or the real-path refusal of an unreadable path. Since realpath-strict-fallback, a check covers the refusal of a looping path. A tracked output under a case-diverged folder is found by file identity; the untracked case needs no identity check on today's git. The lane's independent check found nothing but recorded no probes. On Windows, SIGTERM cleanup and the git-shim fallback have no test, since Windows delivers no SIGTERM and cannot run an extensionless shim.

- Templates on Windows: Copier's update fails when a caller names the project folder by its short 8.3 name, because copier compares it with git's long name. The template-acceptance and release checks put git's whole folder on PATH on Windows, not git alone. Its trace test module is over the template's 500-line cap. Under a fresh home, uvx may pick a Python older than the project's minimum. Nothing tests the Python generator's impact view on Windows with a path written in backslashes.
- readme-check-cp1252: no test runs an adopted Python project's readme check or code map under ASCII or cp1252 output, nor the code map's write mode.

- readme-check-cp1252: since win-post-edit-utf8, post-edit gives Python checks UTF-8 output on every platform. A non-Python checker that writes in a Windows code page is unchanged. Post-edit still reads its output as UTF-8, so a character such as ï or a long dash shows as a replacement mark.
- readme-check-cp1252: the TypeScript readme check claims only paths spelled in ASCII, while the Python one claims any path.
- readme-check-cp1252: both Python checkers were already over the template's 500-line cap, and each grew by three lines.

- Windows skip list (win-leg-blocking): skipping whole desk files hides about 75 checks that pass on Windows. A check now keeps bench files off the list. No check pins which desk files it holds; the Windows CI run is the only evidence.
- Windows skip list (win-leg-blocking): nothing flags a list entry once someone fixes its cause. The list check catches only a removed or renamed file.

- Desk tests on Windows (win-leg-blocking): three skipped desk tests have bugs of their own, still unfixed. Two hand the server a malformed Windows path, and one source scan expects forward slashes. One endpoint check refuses a symlink there with a different error, because of the short temp path. Nobody has tested the desk's pi-root override on Windows. The resolver bug itself is in the desk's known limits.

- Bench on Windows (bench-win): nobody has run the real judge there. An npm install of Claude Code is a script shim the bench cannot start without a shell. The bench then reports the judge unavailable (inferred). Only the missing-judge check and the two command-line checks start a process the platform's own way.

- Bench on Windows (bench-win): nothing checks the bench agent folder's access rights there; its folder-mode check only skips. On a Windows machine without symlink rights, the bench copies the credential, and its symlink check fails by design. CI runners hold those rights.

- Bench judge folder (bench-win): on macOS and Linux the real judge now starts in the user's temp folder, not the fixed one. Nobody re-ran the recorded study labels. The move should not change them, since no project instructions sit above either folder (inferred).
- Desk residuals live in `apps/desk/README.md` Known limits.

- Product report: 37 of the 38 migrated assessments carry an inferred stamp commit, so several show out of date from day one; the installation feature's was refreshed through the guide. "Current" means "matches the stamped ledger", not "rechecked against later decisions". Packets refuse while REQUIREMENTS.md has uncommitted edits. The suite's historical stamp check needs full git history; a shallow clone fails it. No one has yet run the refresh loop with a second model as checker.

- Test details in the report (report-test-details): a test skipped for its platform shows only as this clone's SKIP for its whole file. The page reads no skip reason, no CI Linux or Windows result and no SKIP line inside a file.
- Test details in the report (report-test-details): the label belongs to the whole file, so a PASS file may have skipped the cited check. The page legend says so.
- Test details in the report (report-test-details): the "changed since" mark misses code run from a temporary copy or by a killed child. The page legend says so.
- Test details in the report (report-test-details): a test that carries a row's marker but is not cited in the row's evidence is not listed.
- Test details in the report (report-test-details): no cited test shows its line number.
- Test details in the report (report-test-details): links go to GitHub only. A link to a commit nobody has pushed opens a not-found page.
- Test details in the report (report-test-details): a project with no runtime data, Python projects included, shows every test as having no recorded run.
- Test details in the report (report-test-details): nobody has opened a test link inside the hosted page. The links open a new tab because of a guess that a plain link fails there.

- Test details in the report (review): the new checks read the runtime-data override variable from the caller's environment. Pointed at an empty data file, it turns two checks falsely red. Nothing in the repo sets it for a suite run.

- Test details in the report (review): the page legend's second sentence starts in lower case. The README says "moved" where the code marks a changed or missing file. An origin address ending in a slash gets no link.
- Not-passed list (report-not-passed): a failing test file fixed after the run keeps its row listed, marked changed since, until someone measures again.
- Not-passed list (report-not-passed): a row citing a skipped file beside a file with no recorded run is left out. No such row exists today.
- Not-passed list (report-not-passed): with no runtime data, the list's heading reads 0. The legend just above it says the report found no run.

- Not-passed list (report-not-passed): a label marked changed since still decides the list, so a stale skip keeps its row listed. The plan's adversary called this the claim most likely wrong and left it to the owner. Reversing it changes one rule and flips one requirement.
- Not-passed list (report-not-passed): no check pins that a row citing no test file is never listed. Every check stays green with the empty-run guard removed.

- Requirements tree: no row says the watchdog turns handoff off for every child, yet one share rests on it. Feature statuses miss partial freezes (the compaction store; desk rows in the notices feature). Brief fields and a land-time tree diff come next.

- Tree report: nothing checks that a lane stays inside its named feature. A lane that changes rows in several features still lands; the report names them all. The report reads the ledger text, so a row moved by hand without a tree regeneration shows as moved.

- Watchdog-exit lane: output that a background child of pi writes after pi exits is no longer captured. Before, the watchdog caught it by chance up to one poll later. Real pi's tools use pipes, so this should be rare (inferred).

- Watchdog-exit lane: if pi exits during a CPU read, the watchdog notices only when the read returns. That read takes about a second on Windows. Since win-watchdog-cpu-read, it adds no extra CPU progress line, unless the exit is still unreported after one yield.
- Watchdog-exit lane: no test pins the quick end when pi is missing, or pi-review's quick exit after Ctrl-C. The independent check's probes saw both work.
- Watchdog-exit lane: a pi-worker run with retries and no lane now re-runs a pi killed by a signal. So it repeats that attempt's changes, as it already did after a failed attempt.
- Watchdog-exit lane: its six checks are timing-based, with half a poll interval of margin. A very slow runner could fail them.
- Watchdog-exit lane, found on main too: a review test that kills its launcher leaves one empty capture folder in the temp folder.
- Rulings file: no test proves that a live Claude Code or pi session loads the rulings. The tests stop at the installed file and the prompt section.

- Rulings file: each machine gets the rulings only after one install run after the pull. Until then pi shows the notice, and Claude Code's session start names the missing copy and the install command.
- Rulings file: a Windows copy stays stale until the next install. Doctor and each session start flag it meanwhile.

- Rulings file: on Windows, install now backs up a rulings copy only in four cases (win-copy-backup-noise). The owner edited it, the record is missing or broken, the record does not name it, or the rename fails. Claude Code should not load such a backup as a rule; nobody has tested that.
- Rulings file: every session, builder and reviewer now carries about 600 more tokens.
- Rulings file: no test pins how a model reads the scope sentence. A builder or reviewer may still act on a seat-only ruling, such as pushing its branch.
- Rulings file: the owner and model word lists are short lists, not proofs. Each ruling's wording and scope are the seat's reading of its memory.
- Rulings file: the seat's memory still states the rulings itself. After the land, the seat points its memory at the file.
- Rulings file: on macOS and Linux the pi agent folder holds a link into the checkout. An edit through that link changes the checkout.
- g005-carveout: the export rule stays untested. No check scans modules for a default export; a reviewer reads the rule.

- g005-carveout: a project made from the template gets the new export wording at its next template update. Until it copies the wording into its own ledger, its rail prints one drift line that does not fail. trading-zone needs a follow-up lane in its own repo for that copy.
- g005-carveout: Python projects carry the pi wording too, where it does not apply. It is harmless.
- g005-carveout: on Windows, the rule and skill copies take the new wording only at the next install.
- g005-carveout: the product report's assessment of the engineering-standards feature stays out of date until the queued report refresh.
- Study stop: the run that stopped the study stays a grader-error record, so a resume skips it. Delete its results line to run it again.
- Study stop: a run whose asset copy fails after its child still leaves no evidence on disk. The study now stops there, but nothing writes that run's evidence.
